reference: Donald Trump campaigned on becoming a president unlike any Washington has ever seen. With his inauguration speech, he's already set the tone.

Labour AM Alun Davies criticised the government’s reliance on possible legal action, while Morgan acknowledged that the UK’s intergovernmental arrangements were inadequate and needed reform.

reference: A university has mistakenly emailed hundreds of students intimate and sensitive personal information about dozens of fellow undergraduates.

UEA apologised, launched an urgent investigation, offered support to affected students and notified the Information Commissioner’s Office.

reference: Some progress has been made in encouraging girls to study physics at A-level, according to a report by the Institute of Physics (IoP).

It attributed the persistent gender gap to stereotypes and lack of visibility rather than differences in ability, warning that it limits girls’ career opportunities and contributes to skills shortages in fields such as aerospace and artificial intelligence.

reference: The president of business organisation, the CBI, has said if politicians cannot "get their act together" on Brexit, then the only other option is to "go back to the people".

He called the withdrawal agreement non-negotiable and listed compromise, no deal, or revoking Article 50 as the remaining options, while business groups urged leaders to use the extension to prevent further economic damage and eliminate the risk of no deal.

reference: Ireland's health minister has condemned "reckless scenes" at a venue in Dublin which appeared to breach social distancing regulations.

The venue’s management said it was “absolutely mortified” and closed the premises pending an investigation, while officials warned the incident could worsen the spread of the virus amid rising cases and multiple outbreaks in Ireland.

Amid attacks from Conservatives, Labour MPs and the media, and reports that Ed Miliband was furious, Thornberry resigned from the shadow cabinet after the Rochester by-election polls closed.

reference: The body of a man has been found after a caravan fire in Aberdeenshire.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service extinguished the blaze, and Police Scotland inquiries are ongoing; a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal.

reference: Two more people have been arrested in connection with a fatal shooting.

South Yorkshire Police have arrested six others, including two men detained on suspicion of murder and related offences, while four have been released on bail.

reference: Actor Brian Blessed has announced he will stand for the chancellorship of Cambridge University.
generated: Actor and mountaineer Brian Blessed has secured the 50 nominations needed to challenge supermarket heir Lord Sainsbury in Cambridge University’s chancellor election, after a student-led Facebook campaign. Local shopkeeper Abdul Arain is also seeking nominations, while the winner will succeed the retiring Duke of Edinburgh as the university’s lifelong constitutional head.

reference: The BBC is to feature more arts stories in programmes like The One Show in a bid to make the subject less elitist.
generated: BBC director general Tony Hall will announce new arts commissions, including a modern, digitally enhanced revival of the landmark 1969 series *Civilisation*, in collaboration with the Tate. He will stress the need to engage young people with the arts and expand arts coverage across popular BBC programmes, following a 20% increase in arts funding.

reference: Poorer students in England are up to three A-level grades behind more affluent students, research suggests.
generated: The Education Policy Institute found that disadvantaged students in England start post-16 education behind wealthier peers and fall further behind, averaging a gap equivalent to three A-level grades and up to five in some areas. It attributed the disparity largely to lower GCSE results and disadvantaged students taking fewer or lower-level qualifications, warning the pandemic could worsen the gap and calling for increased funding and targeted support.

reference: Hang out the bunting - well, at least buy a couple of party poppers.
generated: The Bank of England has significantly upgraded its UK growth forecasts since its highly pessimistic post-referendum outlook, supported by stimulus measures, resilient consumer spending and stronger global growth. reference: All MPs are to be automatically offered additional security in their constituency offices and homes.
generated: Amid heightened security concerns following the killing of Labour MP Jo Cox, all MPs will automatically be offered measures such as panic buttons, extra lighting, locks and emergency fobs. The Estimates Committee has removed Ipsa’s authority over security decisions, addressing concerns that its approval process caused delays, while police will continue to handle threat assessments and local security.

reference: With no money left in the government coffers, the "only strategy" for growth is to get behind Britain's entrepreneurs, David Cameron has said.

He called for a shift toward saving, investment, exports and new industries, but Labour accused the Conservatives of offering reheated rhetoric and damaging growth through deep spending cuts and deregulation.

reference: Warcraft's online gaming world is about to get a bit bigger.
generated: World of Warcraft’s fourth expansion, Mists of Pandaria, launches Tuesday, introducing the Asian-themed continent of Pandaria, playable Pandaren characters and a martial-arts monk class. Blizzard hopes the expansion will reverse WoW’s subscriber decline—from over 12 million in 2010 to nine million in June 2012—amid increasing competition from newer and free-to-play games, particularly in China.

reference: The European Central Bank (ECB) has insisted there is still a long way to go before it can call a halt to its economic stimulus programme.

Although the euro briefly rose to a 14-month high after he suggested tapering could be discussed in autumn, Draghi stressed that policymakers want to avoid tightening conditions before wage and price growth strengthen.

reference: South Africa's economic growth slowed sharply in the first three months of the year.
generated: South Africa’s economy grew by just 0.9% in the first quarter, well below expectations and slowing from 2.5% growth last year. Maintenance closures, particularly in the petroleum sector, contributed to the slowdown, while a weak rand and rising inflation complicate the Reserve Bank’s policy decisions.

reference: The UK's biggest bioethanol producer has stopped production at its East Yorkshire plant, blaming government "inaction".
generated: Vivergo Fuels has halted production at its Hull bioethanol plant, warning there is no guarantee it will restart as government delays introducing E10 petrol have increased losses. The shutdown puts 150 employees and about 3,000 supply-chain jobs, including UK farming roles, at risk, though the company plans to conduct maintenance to preserve employment. The Department for Transport says it remains on track to nearly double renewable fuel use by 2020 while considering how to support E10’s introduction.

reference: US President Donald Trump's re-election campaign is running hundreds of Facebook advertisements pushing an unfounded conspiracy theory that Joe Biden cheated during the first US presidential debate.

The baseless rumours spread across social media and conservative outlets before and during the debate, echoing similar unsupported allegations made against presidential candidates in past elections.

reference: The chief executive of the Scottish Police Authority (SPA) is to retire early.
generated: John Foley is expected to leave as chief executive of the Scottish Police Authority in October through early retirement, receiving payment in lieu of notice and an additional settlement. The role is being made redundant as forensic services will report directly to the SPA board, following criticism of the authority’s governance and transparency, while a temporary chief officer is sought.

reference: It was the week when the mobile phone industry's biggest annual trade show was called off over fears about the spread of the coronavirus.

Experts warned that 24-hour news and social platforms can amplify fear and misinformation, although companies such as Google were working with the WHO to promote reliable information.

reference: Wales has the highest take-up of broadband of any of the devolved nations, according to a report from the watchdog Ofcom.
generated: Nearly 79% of premises in Wales can receive superfast broadband, up 24% since 2014, with take-up reaching 77% following substantial public investment through Superfast Cymru. However, Wales had the UK’s lowest 4G availability, while residents watched more television, used more pay-TV and social media, and listened to more radio than people elsewhere in the UK.

reference: Allegations that a police officer falsely claimed to have witnessed former Chief Whip Andrew Mitchell calling police "plebs" are "exceptionally serious", No 10 says.

The Metropolitan Police Federation denied any conspiracy, while the Independent Police Complaints Commission investigates the officer’s claims and CCTV footage that appears to challenge the original police account.

reference: For many Brazilians, Michel Temer's ascension to president was surprising. But as the first Brazilian president to have charges brought against him while in office, his arrest is less unexpected.

Prosecutors accused Temer of leading a long-running bribery scheme, obstructing justice and accepting bribes; he denied the allegations, but was arrested after leaving office and losing legal immunity.

reference: Three siblings have had their stomachs removed after testing positive for a cancer gene following the deaths of their mother and sister.

They say the procedures saved their lives, though they now require smaller, frequent meals and vitamin supplements; Tahir’s 21-year-old daughter has also tested positive for the gene.

reference: The death of a British backpacker in Malaysia remains a mystery six years on, an inquest has heard.
generated: A coroner has concluded that the cause of Gareth Huntley’s death on Malaysia’s Tioman Island in 2014 remains unknown, though she could not rule out third-party involvement and found no evidence supporting it. Huntley’s family said the unresolved circumstances had compounded their grief and left them with many unanswered questions.

reference: The recent high-profile spat with the US over the Hollywood film "The Interview" painted North Korea's enigmatic young leader Kim Jong-un as impetuous.

He also seeks a stronger, more independent economy, reduced reliance on China, and eventual Korean reunification without U.S. influence, though China remains essential to North Korea’s survival and stability.

reference: Saudi Arabia is to allow its women athletes to compete in the Olympics for the first time.
generated: Saudi Arabia will allow women to compete in the Olympics for the first time, with the Olympic Committee overseeing female athletes who qualify. The decision, led by King Abdullah after negotiations with religious leaders, marks a significant but cautious reform despite strong conservative opposition, with athletes expected to wear modest clothing and sports hijabs.

reference: A body has been found in the search for a woman who went missing in floods after her car got stuck in water.

Severe flooding affected hundreds of properties across central and western England, prompting evacuations, major incident declarations, road closures and more than 600 flood warnings at its peak.

reference: High Covid-19 infection rates mean it is "too risky" to allow household support bubbles to be formed on the Isle of Man, the chief minister has told Tynwald.

MHKs highlighted the lockdown’s mental-health effects and urged bubbles for single-parent families, children and key workers.

reference: Prosecutors have said the alleged creator and operator of the Silk Road underground market operated like a traditional drug lord.

Prosecutors say he also solicited murders, though none were carried out, while his lawyers portray him as a scapegoat and deny he operated the site, which was shut down by US authorities in 2013.

reference: Adele has announced a UK tour starting in Leeds next April.

The album is released on 24 January, preceded by “Rolling in the Deep” on 16 January, and reflects her greater maturity and changing perspective since *19*.

reference: Refuge centres have been set up in Oxfordshire as flood warnings on more rivers are put in place.

Oxford has installed flood barriers, while authorities warn of property flooding; a Long Wittenham farmer said 19 vehicles had been rescued from flooded roads after drivers ignored closures.

reference: A man has been arrested on suspicion of murdering a security guard who was stabbed to death at a private party in London's West End on New Year's Day.

Two other security workers and a woman were also injured, while police separately named Charlotte Huggins as the victim of an earlier fatal stabbing in Camberwell.

reference: Rock star Eric Clapton is to sell off part of his extensive guitar collection to raise money for his rehab clinic.

Highlights include a guitar from Cream’s 2005 reunion shows, Marshall cabinets used with Derek and the Dominos, and guitars donated by Jeff Beck, JJ Cale and Joe Bonamassa.

reference: You have to feel the Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) pain.
generated: The OBR has criticised the government for submitting key policy costings late, making its already tight forecasting timetable more difficult. Its chairman also condemned the increasingly complex and opaque spending assumptions used to project expenditure beyond the years covered by detailed plans, warning that these assumptions now have a greater impact on the budget forecast than policy changes themselves.

reference: Nigeria's President Muhammadu Buhari is seeking fresh treatment in London for an undisclosed illness.

His health has raised concerns about a potential power vacuum, although the presidency says government will function normally; before departing, Buhari met 82 Chibok schoolgirls released by Boko Haram.

reference: The Italian government has approved austerity measures worth 24 billion euros (£20bn; $29bn) for the years 2011-2012.

The government aims to reduce its deficit from 5.3% to below 3% of GDP by 2012, but public-sector workers have protested, arguing they have already borne the burden of previous cuts.

reference: A project to support families in Hartlepool affected by separation has been boosted by a £460,778 grant from the Big Lottery Fund (BLF).

Building on a pilot that helped more than 100 families, the project will train parents to support others experiencing family breakdown.

reference: People in Wiltshire are being asked what they would like to see in the county's museum when it moves to its new home in a former courthouse.

The project will include exhibition galleries, a café, shop, storage and community spaces, with a new canal-side extension, while a public survey and consultation invite creative ideas for activities and the building’s future.

reference: Footage has emerged appearing to show tension between Spain's Queen Letizia and her mother-in-law Queen Sofia.

The incident sparked criticism from Spanish media and Marie Chantal of Greece, while reports described longstanding tensions between the two queens over family relationships and access to the princesses.

reference: A public prosecutor and his driver have been killed in the restive south-eastern Iranian province of Sistan Baluchistan, state media say.

The killing followed the deaths of 14 border guards and the execution of 16 alleged regime opponents, though provincial officials said the incidents were unrelated; no group has claimed responsibility for Nouri’s murder.

reference: The Scottish government plans to create a new benefit to help people struggling to pay for funeral costs.
generated: The Scottish government has proposed a Funeral Expense Assistance benefit, planned for summer 2019, to prevent bereaved people facing financial hardship from being pushed into poverty by rising funeral costs. Its 10-point plan also includes advice services, consumer protections, a Social Innovation Fund and a pilot funeral bond to help people save for burial expenses.

reference: Scottish Finance Secretary Derek Mackay has struck a deal to pass his plans for tax and spending for the year ahead at Holyrood. What are the big ideas and spending commitments?

The minority SNP government secured Green Party support for the budget, which is based on forecasts of 1.4% economic growth this year and 1.2% in 2019.

reference: The chairman of the BBC Trust, Lord Patten, has told MPs he had no choice but to agree to a £450,000 pay-off to director general George Entwistle.

He defended Entwistle as a decent man overwhelmed by events and said the BBC must improve investigative journalism standards while restoring public trust after wrongly implicating Lord McAlpine and mishandling allegations concerning Jimmy Savile.

reference: A man who left unwanted furniture including a wardrobe, TVs and bed outside a shut charity shop has landed himself a £1,000 court bill for fly-tipping.

He was fined £420, ordered to pay £567.23 in costs, £60 compensation and a £20 surcharge, as Carmarthenshire Council warned that leaving items outside charity shops can constitute fly-tipping.

reference: A diary detailing a soldier's experience in the Battle of the Somme has been discovered in a barn.

Found among military items in Leicestershire, the diary ends abruptly in October 1916, but research confirmed Diggins survived the war and later became a husband and father.

reference: What makes an entrepreneur? The BBC's Roman Lebed and Tom Santorelli speak to Ruslan Gritsaylo about how he set up a business taking people on paratrike tours in the skies above Kiev.

Because Ukrainian regulations for ultralight aircraft are unclear, he operates in a legal gray area, while expanding revenue through advertising, airshows, and professional flight videos.

reference: The government has said there must be an "unprecedented solution" for the border between Northern Ireland and the Republic after Brexit.

While both governments oppose border infrastructure and some Irish officials welcomed the principles, critics and the EU say the plans lack credible detail and require a political agreement to protect the Good Friday Agreement first.
